newsitem.title: TOGO: OAU leaders secure symbolic first steps on Zaire.
newsitem.headline: OAU leaders secure symbolic first steps on Zaire.

text.p: African leaders, anxious to show they can put their troubled house in order, brought together Zaire's warring parties in Togo for a symbolic first step towards talks on ending the conflict.

A special Organisation of African Unity (OAU) summit in the Togolese capital Lome on Wednesday and Thursday secured a handshake between representatives of the civil war foes and a commitment to future talks and a truce.
At their headquarters in Goma, Zaire, the rebels said on Friday that talks with representatives of ailing President Mobutu Sese Seko would start in South Africa early next week.
"If nothing changes, then the talks will be in South Africa and will begin on either Monday or Tuesday," Moise Nyarugabo, rebel secretary-general told Reuters.
In Johannesburg, a government source confirmed that South Africa had been asked to host peace talks and said senior Foreign Ministry officials had started laying the groundwork.
But even with a date the two sides and mediators still have to resolve the thorny problems of the agenda and a ceasefire.

The rebels of veteran dissident Laurent Kabila hold a quarter of the sprawling Central African nation and are advancing deep inside its key mineral- rich central and southern provinces of Kasai and Shaba. They took up arms last October to topple Mobutu, 66.

Kabila's representatives in Togo, tasting the de facto recognition conferred by an invitation to their first major international forum, addressed the heads of state in closed session -- drawing a strong protest from Kinshasa's delegation.
But they stressed they were not in Togo to negotiate.

"We are very excited to learn that for the first time the people from Kinshasa have decided to agree on a starting of the negotiations which are going to be in a very few days to come," Bizima Karaha, Kabila's foreign affairs strategist, said.

"We are ready to go in any country as long as those Zaireans are serious," Karaha said, adding that the rebels were also happy to sign a truce, but the question was with whom as there was a "political vacuum" in Kinshasa.
"There are some people who have a little power, notably Mobutu and we would like to negotiate with him," he said.
Mobutu, one of Africa's first wave of post-independence military strongmen, has dominated the former Belgian colony since seizing power in 1965.
A combination of prostate cancer surgery in Europe in August, the revolt and the gradual collapse of central authority in Zaire have all but broken his grip.

A dispute over nationality for an ethnic Tutsi minority -- who form the hard core of Kabila's forces -- triggered the revolt which has since rallied a cross section of opponents of the veteran president and won widespread popular acclaim.
Mobutu's despised and ill-disciplined army has collapsed in the face of the rebel advance on several fronts.

Ordinary Zaireans accuse Mobutu and his clan of plundering the wealth of what is potentially one of Africa's richest nations. They are hungry for change -- any change -- from the poverty they have endured under his rule.

The summit, the first organised by the OAU's Central Organ of the Mechanism for Conflict Prevention, Management and Resolution, urged the two sides to hold immediate talks leading to a ceasefire -- a moral victory for Kabila's rebels.
With U.N. Secretary General Kofi Annan playing a full part in the talks, it urged all players to rally round a peace plan formulated by U.N. and OAU special envoy Mohamed Sahnoun.

"The two delegations have reiterated their commitment to accept the principle of a ceasefire and the principle of negotiations," a separate statement issued by host Togo said after separate talks on the sidelines.
The rebels say the talks should focus on Mobutu's departure. "It's in his interest to negotiate his own departure," Kabila representative Gaetan Kakudji said in Lome.
Kabila, who is in a position of strength, has little incentive to negotiate other than international recognition.
Diplomats say that once the fighting halts, the focus will switch to elections to end Zaire's lagging democratic transition -- already seven years old and far from complete.
"Kabila needs legitimacy," one said, adding that elections were the one way to ensure lasting stability.

France and the United States, accused of supporting opposite sides in the war, have called jointly for all-party talks and an agreed electoral process leading to ..."stable, legitimate and recognised institutions".
Meanwhile, Zaire's political family, sensing the winds of change, is desperately trying to adapt.
One member of the Kinshasa delegation scribbled down his name for a journalist adding that he was a member of the transitional parliament and of Mobutu's Popular Revolutionary Movement (MPR).
As an afterthought, he scribbled out the reference to Mobutu's party.
